subproblems.title: Hilbert-Schmidt norm: comparison with the operator norm and triangle inequality
subproblems.statement: For all natural numbers m, k and all continuous linear maps A, B : R^m -> R^k (Rn m ->L[R] Rn k), writing hsNormSq A = sum_{i<m} |A e_i|^2 (e_i = EuclideanSpace.single i 1 the standard basis of R^m), hsNorm A = sqrt(hsNormSq A), and ||A|| for the operator norm: (i) ||A|| <= hsNorm A; (ii) hsNorm A <= sqrt(m) * ||A||; (iii) hsNorm (A + B) <= hsNorm A + hsNorm B.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (m k : ℕ) (A B : Rn m →L[ℝ] Rn k), ‖A‖ ≤ hsNorm A ∧ hsNorm A ≤ Real.sqrt m * ‖A‖ ∧ hsNorm (A + B) ≤ hsNorm A + hsNorm B
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof, step 6 (norm comparison ||A|| <= |A| <= sqrt(n) ||A||), and the norm property of the Hilbert-Schmidt norm |.| used in step 3 (triangle inequality). Here m, k are arbitrary, so the result applies both to maps R^n -> R^l and to operators of R^(n+l) (m = k = n + l).

Notation. e_i := EuclideanSpace.single i 1 (i < m) is the standard orthonormal basis of R^m; a_i := ||A e_i|| >= 0, b_i := ||B e_i|| >= 0. By definition hsNormSq A = sum_i a_i^2 >= 0 and hsNorm A = sqrt(hsNormSq A) >= 0, so (hsNorm A)^2 = hsNormSq A; similarly for B.

1. (i) Let v in R^m with coordinates v_i. Then v = sum_i v_i e_i (expansion in the standard basis, EuclideanSpace.basisFun / sum_repr), hence A v = sum_i v_i (A e_i) by linearity, and by the triangle inequality ||A v|| <= sum_i |v_i| a_i. By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for finite sums, sum_i |v_i| a_i <= (sum_i v_i^2)^(1/2) (sum_i a_i^2)^(1/2) = ||v|| * hsNorm A, using ||v||^2 = sum_i v_i^2 (EuclideanSpace.norm_eq). Thus ||A v|| <= hsNorm A * ||v|| for every v, and since hsNorm A >= 0 the operator-norm bound criterion (ContinuousLinearMap.opNorm_le_bound) gives ||A|| <= hsNorm A.

2. (ii) Each e_i has norm 1, so a_i = ||A e_i|| <= ||A|| ||e_i|| = ||A||, and since 0 <= a_i also a_i^2 <= ||A||^2. Summing over the m indices gives hsNormSq A <= m ||A||^2. The square root is monotone, so hsNorm A = sqrt(hsNormSq A) <= sqrt(m ||A||^2) = sqrt(m) * sqrt(||A||^2) = sqrt(m) * ||A|| (Real.sqrt_mul with m >= 0, and sqrt(t^2) = t for t = ||A|| >= 0).

3. (iii) For each i, ||(A + B) e_i|| = ||A e_i + B e_i|| <= a_i + b_i, and both sides are >= 0, so ||(A + B) e_i||^2 <= (a_i + b_i)^2. Hence hsNormSq (A + B) <= sum_i (a_i + b_i)^2 = sum_i a_i^2 + 2 sum_i a_i b_i + sum_i b_i^2. By Cauchy-Schwarz, sum_i a_i b_i <= (sum_i a_i^2)^(1/2)(sum_i b_i^2)^(1/2) = hsNorm A * hsNorm B. Therefore hsNormSq (A + B) <= (hsNorm A)^2 + 2 hsNorm A hsNorm B + (hsNorm B)^2 = (hsNorm A + hsNorm B)^2. Taking square roots (both hsNorm A + hsNorm B >= 0 and the square root is monotone): hsNorm (A + B) <= hsNorm A + hsNorm B. (Equivalent formal route: hsNorm X is the norm of the vector (X e_i)_i in the L^2 product space PiLp 2 (fun _ : Fin m => Rn k) by PiLp.norm_eq_of_L2; the map X |-> (X e_i)_i is additive, so (iii) is norm_add_le there.)

4. Steps 1, 2 and 3 are the three conjuncts.
proof_key_steps: Expand v in the standard basis; triangle inequality and Cauchy-Schwarz give ||A v|| <= hsNorm A ||v||, hence ||A|| <= hsNorm A
||A e_i|| <= ||A|| for the unit vectors e_i gives hsNormSq A <= m ||A||^2, hence hsNorm A <= sqrt(m) ||A||
Pointwise triangle inequality and Cauchy-Schwarz (Minkowski) give hsNorm (A + B) <= hsNorm A + hsNorm B

subproblems.title: Every n-dimensional subspace of R^(n+l) is a rotated coordinate plane
subproblems.statement: For all natural numbers n, l and every linear subspace T of R^(n+l) = Amb n l with dim T = n, there is a linear isometry equivalence q of R^(n+l) with rotatedPlane q = T, where rotatedPlane q = (horizontalPlane n l).map q and horizontalPlane n l = span{EuclideanSpace.single (Fin.castAdd l i) 1 : i < n} = R^n x {0}.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (T : Submodule ℝ (Amb n ℓ)), Module.finrank ℝ T = n → ∃ q : Amb n ℓ ≃ₗᵢ[ℝ] Amb n ℓ, rotatedPlane q = T
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof, step 7 (rotations).

Notation. E_k := EuclideanSpace.single k 1 (k in Fin (n+l)) is the standard orthonormal basis of R^(n+l) = Amb n l = EuclideanSpace R (Fin (n+l)); the indices Fin.castAdd l i (i < n) are the first n coordinates and Fin.natAdd n j (j < l) the last l. By definition rotatedPlane q = (horizontalPlane n l).map q and horizontalPlane n l = span{E_(castAdd l i) : i < n}.

1. Since finrank T = n, T has an orthonormal basis u_0, ..., u_(n-1) indexed by Fin n (stdOrthonormalBasis R T is indexed by Fin (finrank R T); reindex it along the equality finrank R T = n, e.g. with finCongr). Regard each u_i as a vector of R^(n+l); then (u_i) is an orthonormal family in R^(n+l) whose span is T.

2. The orthogonal complement T^perp has dimension (n + l) - n = l, because finrank T + finrank T^perp = finrank R^(n+l) = n + l (Submodule.finrank_add_finrank_orthogonal, finrank_euclideanSpace_fin). Choose an orthonormal basis u_n, ..., u_(n+l-1) of T^perp. Put b(castAdd l i) := u_i and b(natAdd n j) := u_(n+j). The family (b k)_(k in Fin (n+l)) is orthonormal: vectors from T are orthonormal among themselves, vectors from T^perp are orthonormal among themselves, and every vector of T is orthogonal to every vector of T^perp. It consists of n + l = dim R^(n+l) orthonormal, hence linearly independent, vectors, so it is an orthonormal basis b of R^(n+l) indexed by Fin (n+l) with b(castAdd l i) = u_i for all i < n.
   (Formal shortcut for this step: apply Orthonormal.exists_orthonormalBasis_extension_of_card_eq with index type Fin (n+l), card = n + l = finrank R^(n+l), s := range (Fin.castAdd l), v(castAdd l i) := u_i and v(natAdd n j) := 0 (defined by Fin.addCases). The restriction of v to s is orthonormal because Fin.castAdd l is injective and (u_i) is orthonormal. The lemma yields an orthonormal basis b with b k = v k for k in s, i.e. b(castAdd l i) = u_i.)

3. Let q := b.repr.symm. Here b.repr : R^(n+l) -> EuclideanSpace R (Fin (n+l)) is a linear isometry equivalence, and EuclideanSpace R (Fin (n+l)) is literally Amb n l, so q : Amb n l ≃ₗᵢ[R] Amb n l. It sends the standard orthonormal basis to b: q E_k = b k for every k (OrthonormalBasis.repr_symm_single).

4. Then rotatedPlane q = (span{E_(castAdd l i)}).map q = span{q E_(castAdd l i) : i < n} (Submodule.map_span) = span{b(castAdd l i) : i < n} = span{u_i : i < n} = T, the last equality by step 1: (u_i) is a basis of T, so the span in R^(n+l) of the vectors u_i is the image of T under the inclusion, i.e. T itself.

5. Hence q is a linear isometry equivalence with rotatedPlane q = T.
proof_key_steps: Orthonormal basis u_0..u_(n-1) of T indexed by Fin n (finrank T = n)
Extend to an orthonormal basis b of R^(n+l) indexed by Fin (n+l) with b(castAdd i) = u_i (T plus T^perp, or exists_orthonormalBasis_extension_of_card_eq)
q := b.repr.symm is a linear isometry equivalence with q E_k = b k
rotatedPlane q = span{q E_(castAdd i)} = span{u_i} = T

subproblems.title: (Nor): vertical deviation from a rotated graph plane is controlled by the distance to it
subproblems.statement: For natural numbers n, l, a linear isometry equivalence q of R^(n+l), a continuous linear map A : R^n -> R^l with operator norm ||A|| <= 1, and x in R^n, y in R^l: let Gamma_A = span{graphPoint v (A v) : v in R^n}, K = q(Gamma_A) = Gamma_A.map q, P the orthogonal projection (starProjection) of R^(n+l) onto K, and w = q(graphPoint x y). Then ||y - A x|| <= 2 ||w - P w||.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (q : Amb n ℓ ≃ₗᵢ[ℝ] Amb n ℓ) (A : Rn n →L[ℝ] Rn ℓ) (x : Rn n) (y : Rn ℓ), ‖A‖ ≤ 1 → ‖y - A x‖ ≤ 2 * ‖q (graphPoint x y) - ((Submodule.span ℝ (Set.range fun v : Rn n => graphPoint v (A v))).map q.toLinearEquiv.toLinearMap).starProjection (q (graphPoint x y))‖
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof, step 5 ((Nor)). The parent bounds |y - A x| by (1 + ||A||^2)^(1/2) |graphPoint (x - v) (y - A v)| for every v and takes the infimum over v; here the same estimate is applied at the minimizing point v given by the orthogonal projection, so no infimum is needed.

0. Facts about graphPoint. By definition graphPoint x y = toLp 2 (Fin.append (ofLp x) (ofLp y)), so its coordinate at Fin.castAdd l i is x_i and its coordinate at Fin.natAdd n j is y_j (Fin.append_left, Fin.append_right), and every index of Fin (n+l) has one of these two forms (Fin.addCases). Consequently:
 (a) graphPoint is jointly linear: graphPoint (x + x') (y + y') = graphPoint x y + graphPoint x' y' and graphPoint (c x) (c y) = c graphPoint x y; in particular graphPoint x y - graphPoint x' y' = graphPoint (x - x') (y - y') (compare coordinates);
 (b) ||graphPoint x y||^2 = sum_i x_i^2 + sum_j y_j^2 = ||x||^2 + ||y||^2 (EuclideanSpace.norm_eq together with Fin.sum_univ_add).

1. Let J : R^n -> R^(n+l), J v := graphPoint v (A v). By 0(a) and the linearity of A, J is linear. Hence its range is a subspace, and Gamma_A = span(range J) = range J (Submodule.span_eq applied to LinearMap.range J, whose underlying set is range J by LinearMap.coe_range). So every element of Gamma_A has the form graphPoint v (A v) for some v in R^n.

2. Let w := q(graphPoint x y) and K := Gamma_A.map q; K is finite-dimensional, so its orthogonal projection P exists. P w lies in K (it is the coercion of the element orthogonalProjectionOnto w of K). By the definition of Submodule.map, P w = q z for some z in Gamma_A, and by step 1 z = graphPoint v (A v) for some v in R^n. Fix this v.

3. Then w - P w = q(graphPoint x y) - q(graphPoint v (A v)) = q(graphPoint (x - v) (y - A v)) by linearity of q and 0(a). Since q is an isometry, ||w - P w|| = ||graphPoint (x - v) (y - A v)|| =: d, and by 0(b) d^2 = ||x - v||^2 + ||y - A v||^2, d >= 0.

4. Put a := ||x - v|| >= 0 and c := ||y - A v|| >= 0. Since y - A x = (y - A v) + A(v - x), the triangle inequality and ||A(v - x)|| <= ||A|| ||v - x|| <= ||v - x|| = a (using ||A|| <= 1) give ||y - A x|| <= c + a.

5. (c + a)^2 = a^2 + 2ac + c^2 <= 2(a^2 + c^2) = 2 d^2 <= 4 d^2, because 2ac <= a^2 + c^2 (as (a - c)^2 >= 0). Since c + a >= 0 and 2d >= 0, this gives c + a <= 2 d. (This is the parent's Cauchy-Schwarz estimate (1 + ||A||^2)^(1/2) d <= sqrt 2 d <= 2 d at the point v.)

6. Combining steps 3, 4 and 5: ||y - A x|| <= c + a <= 2 d = 2 ||w - P w||, which is the claim (with w = q(graphPoint x y) and P the starProjection of (span{graphPoint v (A v)}).map q).
proof_key_steps: graphPoint is jointly linear and ||graphPoint x y||^2 = ||x||^2 + ||y||^2
span{graphPoint v (A v)} is the range of the linear map v |-> graphPoint v (A v), so P w = q(graphPoint v (A v)) for some v
||w - P w|| = ||graphPoint (x - v) (y - A v)|| because q is an isometry

subproblems.title: Conjugation by a linear isometry: projections onto rotated subspaces and invariance of hsNormSq
subproblems.statement: Let n, l be natural numbers and q a linear isometry equivalence of R^(n+l); write Q and Q' for q and q^(-1) = q.symm as continuous linear maps of R^(n+l). (a) For every linear subspace K of R^(n+l), the orthogonal projection onto q(K) = K.map q equals Q o p_K o Q', where p_K is the orthogonal projection onto K. (b) For every continuous linear X : R^(n+l) -> R^(n+l), hsNormSq (Q o X o Q') = hsNormSq X (Hilbert-Schmidt norm squared, computed in the standard basis).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (q : Amb n ℓ ≃ₗᵢ[ℝ] Amb n ℓ), (∀ K : Submodule ℝ (Amb n ℓ), (K.map q.toLinearEquiv.toLinearMap).starProjection = q.toLinearIsometry.toContinuousLinearMap ∘L K.starProjection ∘L q.symm.toLinearIsometry.toContinuousLinearMap) ∧ ∀ X : Amb n ℓ →L[ℝ] Amb n ℓ, hsNormSq (q.toLinearIsometry.toContinuousLinearMap ∘L X ∘L q.symm.toLinearIsometry.toContinuousLinearMap) = hsNormSq X
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof, notation paragraph ("its orthogonal projection (starProjection) is P_q(A) = q Pi(A) q^-1" and "Conjugation by a linear isometry preserves |.|"), used in steps 1, 3 and 4 of the parent proof.

Notation. N := n + l; Amb n l = EuclideanSpace R (Fin N); E_k := EuclideanSpace.single k 1 (k in Fin N) is the standard orthonormal basis; <.,.> is the inner product; hsNormSq Y = sum_k ||Y E_k||^2.

1. (a) Every subspace of the finite-dimensional space R^N is complete, so the orthogonal projections onto K and onto K.map q exist. Let z in R^N and u := q(p_K(q^(-1) z)). Then u lies in q(K) = K.map q. For every element q k of q(K) (k in K): <z - u, q k> = <q(q^(-1) z - p_K(q^(-1) z)), q k> = <q^(-1) z - p_K(q^(-1) z), k> = 0, because q preserves inner products and q^(-1) z - p_K(q^(-1) z) is orthogonal to K. By the characterization of the orthogonal projection (Submodule.eq_starProjection_of_mem_of_inner_eq_zero), the projection of z onto q(K) is u = (Q o p_K o Q') z. (This is Mathlib's Submodule.starProjection_map_apply.) As z is arbitrary, the two continuous linear maps are equal; formally ContinuousLinearMap.ext fun z => Submodule.starProjection_map_apply q K z closes (a) (a bare `ext z` would descend to EuclideanSpace coordinates, where the lemma no longer matches).

2. (b), transpose. For e in R^N define X^T e := sum_k <X E_k, e> E_k. For every u in R^N we have u = sum_k <E_k, u> E_k, so by linearity <X u, e> = sum_k <E_k, u> <X E_k, e> = <X^T e, u>.

3. Basis independence. Let (b_k)_(k in Fin N) be any orthonormal basis of R^N. Parseval's identity holds for both (E_j) and (b_k): ||z||^2 = sum_j <E_j, z>^2 = sum_k <b_k, z>^2 for every z (OrthonormalBasis.sum_sq_inner_right). Therefore
 sum_k ||X b_k||^2 = sum_k sum_j <E_j, X b_k>^2 = sum_j sum_k <X^T E_j, b_k>^2 = sum_j ||X^T E_j||^2,
 where the middle equality uses step 2 (<X b_k, E_j> = <X^T E_j, b_k>), the symmetry of the real inner product and the exchange of finite sums, and the last equality is Parseval for (b_k) applied to the vector X^T E_j. The right-hand side does not depend on the orthonormal basis (b_k).

4. Apply step 3 to b_k := q^(-1) E_k, an orthonormal basis since q^(-1) is a linear isometry equivalence (the image of the standard orthonormal basis, OrthonormalBasis.map), and to b_k := E_k. Using also that q is an isometry:
 hsNormSq (Q o X o Q') = sum_k ||q(X(q^(-1) E_k))||^2 = sum_k ||X(q^(-1) E_k)||^2 = sum_j ||X^T E_j||^2 = sum_k ||X E_k||^2 = hsNormSq X.
 This proves (b).
proof_key_steps: The projection onto q(K) is q o p_K o q^-1 (membership plus orthogonality characterization; starProjection_map_apply)
Hand-built transpose X^T e = sum_k <X E_k, e> E_k satisfies <X u, e> = <X^T e, u>
Parseval: sum_k ||X b_k||^2 = sum_j ||X^T E_j||^2 for every orthonormal basis (b_k)
Apply with b = q^-1 E and b = E; q is isometric, so hsNormSq (q X q^-1) = hsNormSq X

subproblems.title: The graph of the zero map is the horizontal plane
subproblems.statement: For all natural numbers n, l: span{graphPoint v (0 v) : v in R^n} = horizontalPlane n l, where 0 : R^n -> R^l is the zero continuous linear map and horizontalPlane n l = span{EuclideanSpace.single (Fin.castAdd l i) 1 : i < n}.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ), Submodule.span ℝ (Set.range fun v : Rn n => graphPoint v ((0 : Rn n →L[ℝ] Rn ℓ) v)) = horizontalPlane n ℓ
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof, step 4 ("graphPoint v 0 = sum_{i<n} v_i e_{castAdd i}, so Gamma_0 = span{e_{castAdd i} : i < n} = horizontalPlane n l").

Notation. E_k := EuclideanSpace.single k 1 in R^(n+l); e_i := EuclideanSpace.single i 1 in R^n.

1. (0 : R^n ->L R^l) v = 0 for every v.

2. Claim: graphPoint v 0 = sum_{i<n} v_i E_(castAdd l i) for every v in R^n. Compare coordinates at k in Fin (n+l), using Fin.addCases. At k = castAdd l i': the left side is v_(i') (definition of graphPoint, Fin.append_left), and the right side is sum_i v_i [castAdd l i = castAdd l i'] = v_(i') because castAdd l is injective. At k = natAdd n j: the left side is the j-th coordinate of 0, i.e. 0 (Fin.append_right), and the right side is sum_i v_i [castAdd l i = natAdd n j] = 0 because castAdd l i has value < n while natAdd n j has value >= n.

3. Inclusion of the graph span in horizontalPlane: by step 2 each generator graphPoint v (0 v) = graphPoint v 0 is a linear combination of the generators E_(castAdd l i) of horizontalPlane n l (Submodule.sum_mem, Submodule.smul_mem, Submodule.subset_span), hence lies in horizontalPlane n l; by Submodule.span_le the whole span is contained in horizontalPlane n l.

4. Reverse inclusion: for i < n, step 2 applied to v = e_i (coordinates delta_(i i')) gives graphPoint e_i 0 = E_(castAdd l i), so E_(castAdd l i) = graphPoint e_i (0 e_i) is a generator of the left span. Thus every generator of horizontalPlane n l lies in the left span, and by Submodule.span_le horizontalPlane n l is contained in it.

5. By antisymmetry of the inclusion order the two subspaces are equal.
proof_key_steps: graphPoint v 0 = sum_i v_i E_(castAdd i), by comparing coordinates
Each generator of either span lies in the other span; conclude by span_le and antisymmetry

subproblems.title: The graph-plane projection map is C^2, with derivative at 0 of Hilbert-Schmidt size sqrt 2
subproblems.statement: For natural numbers n, l let Pi : L(R^n, R^l) -> L(R^(n+l), R^(n+l)) send A to the orthogonal projection (starProjection) of R^(n+l) onto Gamma_A = span{graphPoint v (A v) : v in R^n}, both spaces carrying the operator norm. Then (1) Pi is C^2 (ContDiff R 2), and (2) for every H in L(R^n, R^l), hsNormSq (DPi(0)[H]) = 2 hsNormSq H, where DPi(0) = fderiv R Pi 0.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ), ContDiff ℝ 2 (fun A : Rn n →L[ℝ] Rn ℓ => (Submodule.span ℝ (Set.range fun v : Rn n => graphPoint v (A v))).starProjection) ∧ ∀ H : Rn n →L[ℝ] Rn ℓ, hsNormSq (fderiv ℝ (fun A : Rn n →L[ℝ] Rn ℓ => (Submodule.span ℝ (Set.range fun v : Rn n => graphPoint v (A v))).starProjection) 0 H) = 2 * hsNormSq H
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof, notation paragraph (J_A v = graphPoint v (A v), J_A^* J_A = I + A^*A, Pi(A) = J_A (I + A^*A)^-1 J_A^*), step 1 (Pi is C^infinity: inversion is smooth on invertible operators) and step 2 (DPi(0)[H] = [[0, H^*],[H, 0]], |DPi(0)[H]|^2 = |H^*|^2 + |H|^2 = 2|H|^2). This is Simon's description (p. 123) of the matrix of p_{T G(f)} as [[I, Df],[Df^t, O]] + F(Df) with F(0) = 0, DF(0) = 0. The adjoint ContinuousLinearMap.adjoint is not in the import closure of GMT.Ch05.Submission, so transposes are built from the standard basis below.

Notation. e_i := EuclideanSpace.single i 1 in R^n (i < n); E_k := EuclideanSpace.single k 1 in R^(n+l) (k in Fin (n+l)); V := (Rn n ->L[R] Rn l), W := (Amb n l ->L[R] Amb n l), both normed by the operator norm; Pi(A) := (span R (range fun v => graphPoint v (A v))).starProjection.

0. graphPoint. From graphPoint x y = toLp 2 (Fin.append x y): its castAdd l i coordinate is x_i and its natAdd n j coordinate is y_j (Fin.append_left/right; all indices are of these forms by Fin.addCases). Hence graphPoint is jointly linear and graphPoint x y = iota x + kappa y, where iota x := graphPoint x 0 and kappa y := graphPoint 0 y are continuous linear maps R^n -> R^(n+l) and R^l -> R^(n+l). (Formal route: graphPoint x y = EuclideanSpace.finAddEquivProd.symm (x, y), proved by ext k, Fin.addCases and simp [graphPoint]; then iota := finAddEquivProd.symm ∘L ContinuousLinearMap.inl and kappa := finAddEquivProd.symm ∘L ContinuousLinearMap.inr.) Moreover ||graphPoint x y||^2 = ||x||^2 + ||y||^2 (EuclideanSpace.norm_eq, Fin.sum_univ_add), so iota and kappa are isometric; <iota x, kappa y> = 0; <iota x, E_(castAdd i)> = x_i, <iota x, E_(natAdd j)> = 0, <kappa y, E_(castAdd i)> = 0, <kappa y, E_(natAdd j)> = y_j.

1. Transpose. For a continuous linear L : R^n -> R^(n+l) let L^T := sum_{i<n} (innerSL R (L e_i)).smulRight e_i, i.e. L^T w = sum_i <L e_i, w> e_i. Expanding v = sum_i v_i e_i gives <L^T w, v> = sum_i <L e_i, w> v_i = <w, L v> for all v, w. The map tau : L |-> L^T is R-linear (L |-> innerSL R (L e_i) is linear and smulRight is linear in the functional) and continuous (finite dimension). Formally, build tau as a LinearMap with toFun L := sum_i (innerSL R (L e_i)).smulRight e_i and turn it into a continuous linear map with LinearMap.toContinuousLinearMap. Hence tau is a continuous linear map and in particular C^infinity.

2. Parametrization. For A in V put J_A := iota + kappa o A (continuous linear R^n -> R^(n+l)); by step 0, J_A v = graphPoint v (A v). The map A |-> J_A is the constant iota plus the continuous linear map A |-> kappa o A (ContinuousLinearMap.compL), so it is C^infinity and has derivative H |-> kappa o H at every point. Since J_A is linear, its range is a subspace, so Gamma_A = span(range J_A) = range J_A (Submodule.span_eq, LinearMap.coe_range). Also ||J_A v||^2 = ||v||^2 + ||A v||^2 >= ||v||^2.

3. Gram operator. G_A := J_A^T o J_A in L(R^n, R^n). By step 1, <G_A v, v> = <J_A v, J_A v> = ||J_A v||^2 >= ||v||^2, so G_A v = 0 forces v = 0. Thus G_A is injective, hence (finite dimension; LinearMap.isUnit_iff_ker_eq_bot via ContinuousLinearMap.isUnit_iff_isUnit_toLinearMap) a unit of the complete normed ring L(R^n, R^n). Put R_A := Ring.inverse G_A, so G_A o R_A = R_A o G_A = 1. The map A |-> G_A = tau(J_A) o J_A is C^infinity (composition through the continuous bilinear composition map, ContDiff.clm_comp).

4. Projection formula. Put F(A) := J_A o R_A o J_A^T in W. For w in R^(n+l): F(A) w = J_A(R_A J_A^T w) lies in range J_A = Gamma_A; and for every element J_A v of Gamma_A, <w - F(A) w, J_A v> = <J_A^T w - J_A^T J_A R_A J_A^T w, v> = <J_A^T w - G_A R_A J_A^T w, v> = 0 by step 1 and G_A o R_A = 1. By the characterization of the orthogonal projection (Submodule.eq_starProjection_of_mem_of_inner_eq_zero), Pi(A) w = F(A) w. Hence Pi(A) = F(A) for every A, i.e. Pi = F as functions on V. (The Lean proof of the accepted lemma aetp_starProjection_range_continuousOn, commit 9f89be4c, makes the same identification with the same hand-built transpose.)

5. Smoothness (first conjunct). The ring L(R^n, R^n) is complete, so Ring.inverse is C^infinity at each of its units (contDiffAt_ringInverse; the instance HasSummableGeomSeries holds). Every G_A is a unit (step 3) and A |-> G_A is C^infinity, so A |-> R_A is C^infinity at every A (ContDiffAt.comp), hence C^infinity (contDiff_iff_contDiffAt). Then F, built from the C^infinity maps A |-> J_A, A |-> R_A and A |-> J_A^T = tau(J_A) by composition of operators (ContDiff.clm_comp), is C^infinity, in particular C^2. Since Pi = F (step 4), Pi is C^2.

6. Values at A = 0. J_0 = iota. pi := iota^T satisfies pi w = sum_i <iota e_i, w> e_i = sum_i w_(castAdd i) e_i; in particular pi(iota v) = v, so G_0 = pi o iota = 1 and R_0 = Ring.inverse 1 = 1; moreover pi E_(castAdd i) = e_i and pi E_(natAdd j) = 0.

7. Derivative at 0. Fix H in V. Use the product rule for compositions of operator-valued maps, D(c o d)[H] = Dc[H] o d + c o Dd[H] (HasFDerivAt.clm_comp), and the chain rule.
 (a) DJ(0)[H] = kappa o H, and D(J^T)(0)[H] = tau(kappa o H) = (kappa o H)^T (tau is linear).
 (b) DG(0)[H] = (kappa o H)^T o iota + pi o (kappa o H). Both terms vanish: for v in R^n, (kappa H)^T(iota v) = sum_i <kappa(H e_i), iota v> e_i = 0 and pi(kappa(H v)) = sum_i <iota e_i, kappa(H v)> e_i = 0, because <iota x, kappa y> = 0. So DG(0) = 0 (as a continuous linear map V -> L(R^n, R^n)).
 (c) The derivative of Ring.inverse at the unit 1 is X |-> -(1 X 1) = -X (hasFDerivAt_ringInverse applied to the unit 1 = G_0); by the chain rule DR(0)[H] = -DG(0)[H] = 0.
 (d) Writing F(A) = J_A o (R_A o J_A^T): DF(0)[H] = DJ(0)[H] o R_0 o J_0^T + J_0 o (DR(0)[H] o J_0^T + R_0 o D(J^T)(0)[H]) = kappa o H o pi + iota o (kappa o H)^T.
 Because Pi = F, fderiv R Pi 0 = fderiv R F 0, hence D_H := fderiv R Pi 0 H = kappa o H o pi + iota o (kappa o H)^T. (In block form w.r.t. R^n x R^l this is [[0, H^T],[H, 0]].)

8. Hilbert-Schmidt norm (second conjunct). hsNormSq D_H = sum_{k in Fin (n+l)} ||D_H E_k||^2 = sum_{i<n} ||D_H E_(castAdd i)||^2 + sum_{j<l} ||D_H E_(natAdd j)||^2 (Fin.sum_univ_add).
 - k = castAdd i: pi E_k = e_i and (kappa H)^T E_k = sum_(i') <kappa(H e_(i')), E_(castAdd i)> e_(i') = 0, so D_H E_k = kappa(H e_i) and ||D_H E_k||^2 = ||H e_i||^2 (kappa isometric).
 - k = natAdd j: pi E_k = 0 and (kappa H)^T E_k = sum_(i') <kappa(H e_(i')), E_(natAdd j)> e_(i') = sum_(i') (H e_(i'))_j e_(i'), so D_H E_k = iota(sum_(i') (H e_(i'))_j e_(i')) and ||D_H E_k||^2 = sum_(i') (H e_(i'))_j^2 (iota isometric, coordinates of a vector of R^n).
 Therefore hsNormSq D_H = sum_i ||H e_i||^2 + sum_j sum_(i') (H e_(i'))_j^2 = hsNormSq H + sum_(i') sum_j (H e_(i'))_j^2 = hsNormSq H + sum_(i') ||H e_(i')||^2 = 2 hsNormSq H, exchanging the finite sums and using ||z||^2 = sum_j z_j^2 for z in R^l (EuclideanSpace.norm_eq). This is the second conjunct.
proof_key_steps: graphPoint x y = iota x + kappa y with iota, kappa isometric and mutually orthogonal; J_A = iota + kappa o A parametrizes Gamma_A
Hand-built transpose L^T w = sum_i <L e_i, w> e_i; the Gram operator G_A = J_A^T J_A >= I is a unit
Pi(A) = J_A G_A^-1 J_A^T by the orthogonality characterization of starProjection; Pi is C^infinity by contDiffAt_ringInverse
At 0: G_0 = 1, DG(0) = 0, D(inverse o G)(0) = 0, so DPi(0)[H] = kappa H pi + iota (kappa H)^T
On the standard basis: hsNormSq DPi(0)[H] = |H|^2 + |H^T|^2 = 2 hsNormSq H

subproblems.title: (Gp) for unrotated graph planes: two-sided Hilbert-Schmidt comparison near 0
subproblems.statement: For all natural numbers n, l there is L_0 with 0 < L_0 <= 1/4 such that for all continuous linear A, B : R^n -> R^l with hsNorm A <= L_0 and hsNorm B <= L_0: hsNormSq (A - B) <= hsNormSq (Pi(A) - Pi(B)) <= 3 hsNormSq (A - B), where Pi(A) is the orthogonal projection (starProjection) of R^(n+l) onto span{graphPoint v (A v) : v in R^n}.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ), ∃ L₀ : ℝ, 0 < L₀ ∧ L₀ ≤ 1 / 4 ∧ ∀ (A B : Rn n →L[ℝ] Rn ℓ), hsNorm A ≤ L₀ → hsNorm B ≤ L₀ → hsNormSq (A - B) ≤ hsNormSq ((Submodule.span ℝ (Set.range fun v : Rn n => graphPoint v (A v))).starProjection - (Submodule.span ℝ (Set.range fun v : Rn n => graphPoint v (B v))).starProjection) ∧ hsNormSq ((Submodule.span ℝ (Set.range fun v : Rn n => graphPoint v (A v))).starProjection - (Submodule.span ℝ (Set.range fun v : Rn n => graphPoint v (B v))).starProjection) ≤ 3 * hsNormSq (A - B)
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof, step 3 ((Gp)) with q = identity; Simon p. 123 (|F(p1) - F(p2)| <= C(|p1| + |p2|)|p1 - p2|, "provided we choose L_0 small enough, depending only on n, l"). Sibling results used:
 [S1] allard52_gpa_hsNorm_bounds: for all m, k and X, Y : Rn m ->L Rn k, ||X|| <= hsNorm X, hsNorm X <= sqrt(m) ||X||, hsNorm (X + Y) <= hsNorm X + hsNorm Y.
 [S2] allard52_gpa_graphProj_smooth: Pi is C^2 on V := (Rn n ->L Rn l) and hsNormSq (DPi(0)[H]) = 2 hsNormSq H for all H, where DPi(0) := fderiv R Pi 0.
The parent measures DPi with norms built from |.|; here we use the operator norms ||.|| of V and W := (Amb n l ->L Amb n l) and convert with [S1], the factor sqrt(n + l) being absorbed into C_g.

0. Elementary facts: hsNorm X >= 0; (hsNorm X)^2 = hsNormSq X (hsNormSq is a sum of squares, Real.sq_sqrt); hsNorm (-X) = hsNorm X (||(-X) e_i|| = ||X e_i||).

1. Lipschitz derivative. By [S2], Pi is differentiable and fderiv R Pi is C^1 (ContDiff.fderiv_right with 1 + 1 <= 2). The closed unit ball B_1 := closedBall 0 1 of the finite-dimensional space V is convex and compact, so fderiv R Pi is Lipschitz on B_1 with some constant K >= 0 (ContDiffOn.exists_lipschitzOnWith): ||DPi(X) - DPi(Y)|| <= K ||X - Y|| for X, Y in B_1. In particular ||DPi(X) - DPi(0)|| <= K ||X|| whenever ||X|| <= 1 (the parent's bound ||DPi(X) - DPi(0)|| <= C_g |X|).

2. Choice of L_0. Put C_g := 1 + sqrt(n + l) K >= 1 and L_0 := min{1/4, (sqrt 3 - sqrt 2)/C_g}. Since sqrt 2 < sqrt 3, L_0 > 0; also L_0 <= 1/4 <= 1 and C_g L_0 <= C_g (sqrt 3 - sqrt 2)/C_g = sqrt 3 - sqrt 2. L_0 depends only on n and l.

3. Let A, B in V with hsNorm A <= L_0 and hsNorm B <= L_0. By [S1], ||A|| <= hsNorm A <= L_0 and ||B|| <= L_0, so A and B lie in S := closedBall 0 L_0, a convex subset of B_1.

4. Mean value inequality. Let D := DPi(0) (a continuous linear map V -> W) and g(X) := Pi(X) - D X. Then g is differentiable with fderiv R g X = DPi(X) - D, and for X in S step 1 gives ||fderiv R g X|| <= K ||X|| <= K L_0. By the mean value inequality on the convex set S (Convex.norm_image_sub_le_of_norm_fderiv_le), ||g A - g B|| <= K L_0 ||A - B||.

5. Remainder. Put R := g A - g B. By linearity of D, Pi(A) - Pi(B) = D(A - B) + R. Let h := hsNorm (A - B) >= 0. Using [S1] with m = k = n + l for R in W and with m = n, k = l for A - B in V:
 hsNorm R <= sqrt(n + l) ||R|| <= sqrt(n + l) K L_0 ||A - B|| <= sqrt(n + l) K L_0 h <= C_g L_0 h <= (sqrt 3 - sqrt 2) h.

6. First-order term. By [S2], hsNormSq (D(A - B)) = 2 hsNormSq (A - B); taking square roots, hsNorm (D(A - B)) = sqrt 2 * h.

7. Upper bound. By the triangle inequality [S1], hsNorm (Pi(A) - Pi(B)) <= hsNorm (D(A - B)) + hsNorm R <= sqrt 2 h + (sqrt 3 - sqrt 2) h = sqrt 3 h. Both sides are >= 0, so squaring and step 0 give hsNormSq (Pi(A) - Pi(B)) <= 3 h^2 = 3 hsNormSq (A - B).

8. Lower bound. D(A - B) = (Pi(A) - Pi(B)) + (-R), so by [S1] and step 0, sqrt 2 h = hsNorm (D(A - B)) <= hsNorm (Pi(A) - Pi(B)) + hsNorm R <= hsNorm (Pi(A) - Pi(B)) + (sqrt 3 - sqrt 2) h. Hence hsNorm (Pi(A) - Pi(B)) >= (2 sqrt 2 - sqrt 3) h >= h, since 2 sqrt 2 - sqrt 3 >= 1: indeed sqrt 3 <= 2 gives (1 + sqrt 3)^2 = 4 + 2 sqrt 3 <= 8 = (2 sqrt 2)^2, so 1 + sqrt 3 <= 2 sqrt 2. Squaring (h >= 0): hsNormSq (A - B) = h^2 <= hsNormSq (Pi(A) - Pi(B)).

9. Steps 2, 7 and 8 prove the statement with this L_0 (for every n, l; the hypothesis n >= 1 of the parent is not needed).
proof_key_steps: fderiv Pi is C^1, hence K-Lipschitz on the compact convex closed unit ball of V
L_0 := min{1/4, (sqrt 3 - sqrt 2)/C_g} with C_g := 1 + sqrt(n + l) K
Mean value inequality for g = Pi - DPi(0) on closedBall 0 L_0 bounds R = g A - g B in operator norm; convert to hsNorm with sqrt(n + l)
hsNorm (DPi(0)(A - B)) = sqrt 2 hsNorm (A - B)
Triangle inequality: (2 sqrt 2 - sqrt 3) h <= hsNorm (Pi(A) - Pi(B)) <= sqrt 3 h, then square
